title: Figure 1 — Hierarchical approach to the selection of the baseline SCr value (adults)
description:
Figure 1 (KDIGO 2026, p.16) describes a hierarchical decision framework for selecting the appropriate baseline serum creatinine (SCr) or cystatin C value when characterizing an AKI event in ADULTS. The hierarchy is used as instructed in Practice Point 1.1.3.

The approach proceeds as follows (in priority order):
1. FIRST CHOICE — Use a representative primary care/outpatient SCr or cystatin C value that reflects the stable clinical state. This should ideally be the mean, median, or most recent value obtained 8 to 365 days before hospital admission or the acute event.
2. SECOND CHOICE — If no outpatient value is available within the past year, use the admission SCr, unless AKI is suspected on admission (e.g., community-acquired AKI).
3. THIRD CHOICE — Use the minimum SCr value during the current admission (including post-AKI values), allowing retrospective AKI diagnosis. This is less desirable due to fluctuations from fluid administration or medications.
4. LAST RESORT — If no measurements are available, back-calculate an estimated baseline using an assumed eGFR of 75 ml/min per 1.73 m2 using a validated eGFR estimating equation (e.g., CKD-EPI). Note: this approach does not account for individual patient characteristics or underlying CKD and may lead to over- or underestimation of AKI.

Key abbreviations in the figure: AKI = acute kidney injury; Cys C = cystatin C; eGFR = estimated glomerular filtration rate; RRT = renal replacement therapy; SCr = serum creatinine.

Source: KDIGO-2026-AKI-AKD-Guideline-Public-Review-Draft-March-2026.pdf, Figure 1, p.16

title: Figure 3 — Hierarchical approach to the selection of the baseline SCr value (children)
description:
Figure 3 (KDIGO 2026, p.19) describes the hierarchical decision framework for selecting the baseline SCr or cystatin C value when characterizing an AKI event in CHILDREN (excluding neonates), as instructed by Practice Point 1.6.2.1.

The hierarchy for children differs from adults in the time window and fallback equations:
1. FIRST CHOICE — Use a representative outpatient SCr that reflects the mean, median, or most recent value within 3 months of admission or the acute event (note: shorter window than adults).
2. SECOND CHOICE — Use age-based creatinine estimating equations (e.g., Schwartz equation using height, or the Pottel Q-age equation which does not require height).
3. THIRD CHOICE — Use normative age-based SCr values from healthy children population ranges.
4. LAST RESORT — Use the nadir SCr (lowest measured during hospitalization); least preferred due to risk of underestimation in critical illness.

Key notes for children:
- Kidney function changes more dynamically in children than adults, requiring a shorter reference window (3 months vs. 365 days).
- Age-specific reference ranges must be used when cystatin C is used to detect AKI in children, as levels vary with age (especially during infancy and puberty).
- Neonates use a separate, dedicated staging system (Table 13) — this figure does NOT apply to neonates.

Key abbreviations: AKI = acute kidney injury; Cys C = cystatin C; eGFR = estimated glomerular filtration rate; RRT = renal replacement therapy; SCr = serum creatinine.

Source: KDIGO-2026-AKI-AKD-Guideline-Public-Review-Draft-March-2026.pdf, Figure 3, p.19

title: Figure 2 — AKD, AKI, and kidney disease outcomes
description:
Figure 2 (KDIGO 2026, p.55) is a conceptual diagram illustrating the relationship and clinical trajectories between Acute Kidney Disease (AKD), Acute Kidney Injury (AKI), and longer-term kidney disease outcomes.

Key concepts illustrated:
- AKD is nearly 3 times as prevalent as AKI. A patient can have AKD without meeting the full criteria for AKI if the GFR decline is too small or too slow.
- The possible disease trajectories are: No Kidney Disease (NKD) → AKI → AKD → CKD → Kidney Failure (GFR <15 or RRT).
- AKD without AKI is independently associated with CKD, requirement for RRT, Major Adverse Kidney Events (MAKE), increased length of hospital stay, and mortality.
- AKD duration is defined as ≤3 months. Events persisting beyond 3 months are reclassified as CKD.
- Recovery is possible at each stage; the figure shows bidirectional arrows between states to represent that resolution can occur.

Abbreviations: AKD = acute kidney disease; AKI = acute kidney injury; CKD = chronic kidney disease; GFR = glomerular filtration rate; NKD = no kidney disease.

Source: KDIGO-2026-AKI-AKD-Guideline-Public-Review-Draft-March-2026.pdf, Figure 2, p.55

title: Figure 5 — Conceptual framework for AKI risk stratification
description:
Figure 5 (KDIGO 2026, p.68) illustrates the conceptual framework for AKI risk stratification, showing how patient susceptibilities interact with acute exposures to determine AKI risk.

Key elements of the framework:
- SUSCEPTIBILITIES (patient-level factors that increase baseline vulnerability): advanced age, CKD, diabetes mellitus, heart failure, liver disease, cancer, hypovolemia, sepsis, low albumin, female sex.
- EXPOSURES (acute triggers that can precipitate AKI in susceptible patients): dehydration, infections, trauma, burns, major surgery, shock, nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast agents, vancomycin), poisons and toxins.
- The framework emphasizes that susceptibilities and exposures interact in non-linear ways — a patient may tolerate a contrast agent under normal conditions but develop AKI when also hypovolemic or with pre-existing CKD.
- Risk stratification tools (e.g., validated clinical models, tubular stress biomarkers such as [TIMP-2]×[IGFBP7], UACR) can identify the highest-risk patients for targeted preventive interventions.
- The right patient, right time, right care approach: risk stratification should inform targeted interventions to reduce the risk of AKI, optimize early recognition, and plan subsequent management.

Source: KDIGO-2026-AKI-AKD-Guideline-Public-Review-Draft-March-2026.pdf, Figure 5, p.68

title: Figure 6 — Pre- and post-implementation pathways for clinical AKI risk models
description:
Figure 6 (KDIGO 2026, p.92) illustrates the required steps before and after implementing an AKI clinical risk model in an electronic health record (EHR), adapted from Quickfall et al. 2024.

PRE-IMPLEMENTATION steps (left side of figure):
1. Define the clinical question and target population (e.g., ICU patients, cardiac surgery patients).
2. Develop or identify a validated AKI prediction model using local data.
3. Validate the model externally in your specific institution's patient population.
4. Assess calibration and discrimination performance across relevant risk strata.
5. Engage IT infrastructure and ensure EHR data harmonization (standardized coding, lab units, timestamps).
6. Train clinical staff and establish a structured response protocol before going live.

POST-IMPLEMENTATION steps (right side of figure):
1. Monitor real-world model performance continuously.
2. Reassess calibration-in-the-large and across risk strata periodically to detect model drift.
3. Update the model when patient populations, clinical practices, or data capture changes.
4. Evaluate alert fatigue and clinical response rates.
5. Measure patient-centered outcomes (mortality, RRT requirement, AKI stage progression).

Key principle: Electronic AKI alerts without a structured clinical response protocol have NOT been shown to improve patient outcomes (Recommendation 2.2.1 recommends AGAINST interruptive SCr-based alerts delivered in isolation).

Abbreviations: AKI = acute kidney injury; ICU = intensive care unit; IT = information technology.

Source: KDIGO-2026-AKI-AKD-Guideline-Public-Review-Draft-March-2026.pdf, Figure 6, p.92

title: Figure 8 — CKD staging by eGFR and UACR categories and AKI risk (forest plot / heat map)
description:
Figure 8 (KDIGO 2026, p.106) is a heat map / forest plot from a meta-analysis of 1.28 million participants showing the adjusted hazard ratios for AKI across different combinations of eGFR and UACR (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio) categories.

Key findings illustrated:
- Both lower eGFR AND higher UACR independently and additively increase AKI risk.
- The grid compares eGFRcr categories (≥90, 60-89, 45-59, 30-44, 15-29 ml/min per 1.73 m2) against UACR categories (normal, mildly increased, moderately increased, severely increased albuminuria).
- Darker green color = lower risk (closer to no CKD reference cell). The reference cell is defined as the proportion of cells without CKD (eGFR ≥60 ml/min per 1.73 m2 and ACR in normal range).
- Numbers in each cell represent the adjusted hazard ratio for AKI compared to the reference cell.
- Adjustment variables included: age, sex, smoking status, systolic blood pressure, total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, BMI, antihypertensive medications, and medical history of diabetes, coronary heart disease, stroke, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, peripheral artery disease, cancer, and COPD.
- Key clinical implication: Measuring UACR at baseline provides ADDITIONAL prognostic value beyond eGFR alone for identifying patients at high AKI risk (Practice Point 2.4.1).

Abbreviations: AKI = acute kidney injury; CKD = chronic kidney disease; eGFRcr = eGFR by creatinine; UACR = urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio.

Source: KDIGO-2026-AKI-AKD-Guideline-Public-Review-Draft-March-2026.pdf, Figure 8, p.106

title: Figure 9 — Multicomponent kidney protection strategy for AKI prevention and management (KEY CLINICAL FLOWCHART)
description:
Figure 9 (KDIGO 2026, p.159) illustrates the multicomponent kidney-protection strategy for the prevention and management of AKI. This is Recommendation 3.2.3 (Grade 1B) — recommended for adult surgical patients at high risk for AKI identified by clinical factors and biomarkers.

The strategy comprises the following core components (to be implemented together as a bundle):

1. HEMODYNAMIC OPTIMIZATION
   - Maintain adequate mean arterial pressure (MAP) — target MAP >65 mmHg in critically ill adults
   - Avoid hypotension during and after surgery
   - Use functional hemodynamic monitoring where available
   - Consider discontinuation of ACE inhibitors (ACEi) and angiotensin-receptor blockers (ARBs) perioperatively in high-risk patients

2. VOLUME STATUS MANAGEMENT
   - Assess and optimize fluid balance before, during, and after surgery
   - For elective major abdominal surgery: liberal fluid strategy aiming for +1–2 kg at 24 hours post-surgery is preferred over restrictive strategy (Recommendation 3.1.4, Grade 1B)
   - Avoid both fluid overload and hypovolemia

3. NEPHROTOXIN AVOIDANCE / MINIMIZATION
   - Review and discontinue nephrotoxic medications when clinically safe (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, vancomycin, contrast agents)
   - Implement nephrotoxin stewardship (daily dynamic prescribing review)
   - Use alternatives to iodinated contrast when possible in high-risk patients

4. GLYCEMIC CONTROL
   - Maintain normoglycemia (avoid both hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia)
   - Note: increased insulin requirements to maintain normoglycemia increase hypoglycemia risk

5. KIDNEY FUNCTION MONITORING
   - Serial monitoring of SCr and urine output
   - Use tubular stress biomarkers (e.g., [TIMP-2]×[IGFBP7]) to identify high-risk patients for targeted intervention
   - In settings without biomarker access, use validated clinical risk scores

EVIDENCE BASE:
- Meta-analysis of 5 RCTs (n=1946 critically ill or surgical adults): multicomponent strategy reduced Stage 2 or 3 AKI (OR: 0.67; 95% CI: 0.56–0.79) and MAKE90 (OR: 0.80; 95% CI: 0.67–0.94) vs usual care.
- PrevAKI multicenter RCT: 14.0% vs 23.9% moderate/severe AKI (adjusted risk reduction 10.0%; p=0.034) in biomarker-enriched cardiac surgery patients.
- BigpAK-2 multicenter RCT (n=1180): kidney-protection strategy in high-risk adults reduced Stage 2/3 AKI after major surgery.

Source: KDIGO-2026-AKI-AKD-Guideline-Public-Review-Draft-March-2026.pdf, Figure 9, p.159

title: Figure 11 — Classifying drugs that potentially cause AKI
description:
Figure 11 (KDIGO 2026, p.209) presents an iterative 4-category classification framework for drugs that have the potential to cause AKI or AKD, based on assessment of kidney function and damage biomarkers at the time of drug exposure. Referenced in Practice Point 4.1.1.

The 4 categories are:

1. NEITHER dysfunction NOR damage — Drug affects SCr concentration via non-kidney mechanisms but does NOT cause actual GFR decline or structural kidney damage.
   - Examples: trimethoprim, cimetidine (block tubular secretion of creatinine, raising SCr without true GFR change)

2. DYSFUNCTION without damage — Drug causes hemodynamic reduction in GFR (functional change) without structural kidney injury.
   - Examples: ACE inhibitors (ACEi), angiotensin-receptor blockers (ARBs), NSAIDs, SGLT2 inhibitors
   - Note: Many of these drugs confer proven outcome benefits despite causing transient SCr rise

3. DAMAGE without dysfunction — Drug causes structural tubular or parenchymal damage measurable by biomarkers, without initial GFR decline.
   - Examples: aminoglycosides, acyclovir, vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) antagonists

4. BOTH dysfunction AND damage — Drug causes both functional GFR decline AND structural kidney damage.
   - Examples: NSAIDs (in high-dose or prolonged use), certain nephrotoxic combinations

Key principles of the classification:
- The categories are DYNAMIC — initial tubular damage without dysfunction can progress to AKI with both dysfunction and damage.
- Risk is modulated by: deleterious risk modifiers (duration, drug burden, hypotension, pharmacokinetic interactions) and risk mitigating interventions (daily dynamic prescribing, kidney function monitoring, patient education).
- Underlying susceptibility factors (Table 14, Chapter 2) determine final clinical impact.

Source: KDIGO-2026-AKI-AKD-Guideline-Public-Review-Draft-March-2026.pdf, Figure 11, p.209

title: Figure 12 — Approach to risk assessment for CA-AKI with contrast imaging
description:
Figure 12 (KDIGO 2026, p.35) is a decision algorithm for assessing and managing the risk of contrast-associated AKI (CA-AKI) before diagnostic or interventional contrast imaging procedures. Referenced in Practice Point 4.9.1.1.

The risk assessment and decision pathway proceeds as follows:

STEP 1 — ASSESS RISK:
- Screen all patients for pre-existing risk factors for CA-AKI:
  Patient-related: reduced GFR (especially eGFR <30 ml/min per 1.73 m2), CKD, diabetes, heart failure, volume depletion, prior AKI, use of concurrent nephrotoxins.
  Procedure-related: high-osmolar contrast media, large contrast volume, intra-arterial administration.

STEP 2 — WEIGH BENEFITS vs. RISKS:
- If the clinical benefit of the contrast procedure exceeds the risk of CA-AKI: proceed with the procedure (do not defer or delay).
- If risk is high: use alternative imaging methods (e.g., ultrasound, MRI without gadolinium) where clinically appropriate.

STEP 3 — RISK MITIGATION (for high-risk patients who proceed):
- Use iso-osmolar or low-osmolar iodinated contrast (Practice Point 4.9.1.2).
- Use the lowest possible contrast dose.
- Avoid dehydration. Provide IV hydration with 0.9% isotonic saline (Recommendation 4.9.2.1, Grade 1B).
- Hold diuretics during isotonic crystalloid administration.
- Do NOT routinely use N-acetylcysteine, ascorbic acid, furosemide, dopamine, or fenoldopam — no consistent benefit shown.
- Do NOT perform prophylactic pericontrast hemodialysis — potentially harmful.
- For patients on metformin with eGFR ≤30 ml/min per 1.73 m2: hold metformin at time of contrast and restart only ≥48 hours later if GFR remains stable.

Source: KDIGO-2026-AKI-AKD-Guideline-Public-Review-Draft-March-2026.pdf, Figure 12, p.35

title: Figure 19 — Options for combining ECMO and CRRT circuits
description:
Figure 19 (KDIGO 2026, p.309) illustrates the technical options for combining Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO) with Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy (CRRT) circuits in critically ill patients requiring both cardiac/respiratory support and kidney replacement therapy.

The 3 main circuit integration options illustrated:

OPTION A — IN-LINE HEMOFILTER integrated into the ECMO circuit:
- A hemofilter is integrated directly into the ECMO circuit itself.
- Replacement fluid is administered.
- Advantage: avoids the need for a separate vascular access for CRRT.
- Disadvantage: less precise fluid management control, flow is dependent on ECMO circuit pressures.

OPTION B — CRRT machine connected in series to the ECMO circuit:
- The CRRT circuit draws blood from and returns blood to the ECMO circuit.
- Provides full CRRT functionality with more precise fluid and solute management.
- Advantage: allows use of full CRRT modalities (CVVH, CVVHD, CVVHDF).

OPTION C — INDEPENDENT CRRT with separate vascular access:
- CRRT runs on its own circuit with its own vascular access (e.g., a second dialysis catheter).
- Most hemodynamically independent option.
- Disadvantage: requires additional vascular access with associated risks.

Key clinical considerations:
- Appropriate clinical oversight is required to support safe circuit integration.
- ECMO circuit pressures affect CRRT blood flow; anticoagulation management is complex.
- Choice of integration method depends on institutional expertise and clinical stability of the patient.

Source: KDIGO-2026-AKI-AKD-Guideline-Public-Review-Draft-March-2026.pdf, Figure 19, p.309

title: Figure 21 — 6-variable risk score to predict transition to severe CKD after AKI
description:
Figure 21 (KDIGO 2026, p.333) presents a 6-variable clinical risk score that predicts transition to severe CKD (G4 or G5, eGFR <30 ml/min per 1.73 m2) in adults following hospitalization with AKI.

The 6 predictor variables in the risk score are:
1. Age (older age = higher risk)
2. Baseline eGFR before the AKI episode (lower baseline = higher risk)
3. AKI severity stage (Stage 2/3 = higher risk than Stage 1)
4. Presence of diabetes mellitus
5. Presence of heart failure
6. Degree of proteinuria/albuminuria at or after the AKI episode

How to use the score:
- Each variable contributes a weighted point value.
- The total score maps to a predicted probability of CKD G4/G5 transition within a defined follow-up period.
- Higher scores identify patients who warrant early nephrology referral and closer post-discharge kidney function monitoring.

Clinical application (Practice Points in Chapter 6):
- Use at hospital discharge to stratify patients for post-AKI follow-up intensity.
- High-risk patients: measure eGFR, UACR, and electrolytes within 3 months of discharge.
- Moderate-risk patients: nephrology follow-up within 6 months.
- All patients with AKI: at minimum one follow-up kidney function assessment within 3 months of discharge.

Source: KDIGO-2026-AKI-AKD-Guideline-Public-Review-Draft-March-2026.pdf, Figure 21, p.333

title: Figure 22 — Proposed framework for AKI/AKD follow-up after hospital discharge
description:
Figure 22 (KDIGO 2026, p.338) presents the proposed follow-up framework for patients after hospitalization with AKI or AKD, organized by risk stratification to guide post-discharge care planning.

FOLLOW-UP FRAMEWORK STRUCTURE:

ALL PATIENTS with AKI or AKD at discharge:
- Assess: eGFR, UACR, electrolytes, blood pressure
- Ensure awareness of AKI episode is communicated to primary care and outpatient providers
- Resume medications withheld during AKI (e.g., RASi, metformin, SGLT2i) with reassessment of kidney function once stable

STRATIFICATION BY RISK (using Figure 21 risk score):

LOW RISK (resolved AKI, normal baseline eGFR, no comorbidities):
- Follow-up with primary care within 3 months
- Assess kidney function (eGFR, UACR) at the 3-month visit

MODERATE RISK (Stage 1–2 AKI, CKD G1–G3a, controlled comorbidities):
- Follow-up with primary care or general nephrology within 3 months
- Repeat eGFR and UACR at 3 and 12 months

HIGH RISK (Stage 3 AKI, CKD G3b–G5, RRT during hospitalization, or high risk score):
- Early nephrology referral within 3 months of discharge
- Comprehensive kidney health assessment including eGFR, UACR, electrolytes, blood pressure, review of medications
- Individualized CKD management plan

SPECIAL POPULATIONS:
- Children: assess global functional status, growth parameters, and neurodevelopmental status at discharge and follow-up visits
- Patients on RRT: individualized follow-up including assessment of RRT dependency vs. recovery potential

Abbreviations: AKD = acute kidney disease; AKI = acute kidney injury; CKD = chronic kidney disease; eGFR = estimated glomerular filtration rate; RASi = renin-angiotensin system inhibitors; RRT = renal replacement therapy; SGLT2i = SGLT2 inhibitors; UACR = urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio.

Source: KDIGO-2026-AKI-AKD-Guideline-Public-Review-Draft-March-2026.pdf, Figure 22, p.338
